wm11658.full:
Introduction

Author: Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian (AS)

Section: Part 1: Islam

It is foolish to imagine that religion means a few things that are mentioned in the Gospel. All matters that are essential for the perfection of man are comprehended

within the scope of religion. Religion comprises all those matters which lead man from his wild condition to the condition of true humanity and then lead him from the condition of humanity to a life of wisdom and thereafter lead him from a life of wisdom to a life that is devoted to
God.

[Kitab-ul-Bariyyah, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 13, p. 89]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 12]

There is no doubt that the Gospel does not provide for the full nurture of the tree of humanity. We are sent into the world with many faculties and every faculty demands that it should be used on its proper occasion. The Gospel emphasizes only the faculty of meekness and gentleness.
Meekness and forgiveness are good qualities when exercised on the proper occasion but their use on every occasion would be greatly harmful. Our cultural life, which comprises the interplay of different kinds of tempers, demands that we should exercise all our faculties with discretion on the proper occasion. It is true that, on some occasions, forgiveness and forbearance would benefit materially and spiritually a person who has done us harm. On other occasions, the exercise of those faculties would encourage the offender to commit greater mischief and to do more harm.

Our spiritual life resembles our physical life to a large degree. It is our experience that the use of only one type of food and medicines would upset our health. If we were to confine ourselves over a period to the use of cooling articles of diet and refrain altogether from the use of warming articles, we would become a prey to some diseases like paralysis, Parkinson’s disease or epilepsy. On the contrary, if we confine ourselves to warming articles of diet, so much so that even the water that we drink

must be warm, then equally we would be liable to some other kind of disease. Consequently, in order to maintain our physical health we must keep a balance between hot and cold, hard and soft, and movement and rest. We should follow the same rule in respect of our spiritual health. God has bestowed no evil faculty upon us. Indeed no faculty is evil in itself; it is the misuse of a faculty that is evil. For instance, envy is evil but if we use it for a good purpose, that is to say, as a competition in goodness, it becomes a high moral quality. The same is the case with all moral qualities. Their misuse renders them harmful and their use on proper occasion in a moderate manner makes them beneficial.

It is, therefore, a mistake to cut off all other branches of the tree of humanity and to put the entire emphasis on forgiveness and forbearance. That is why this teaching has failed in its purpose and Christian sovereigns had to enact codes of law for the punishment of offenders. The current Gospels cannot bring about the perfection of the human self. As the stars are dimmed when the sun rises and then disappear from sight altogether, the same is the case of the Gospel in comparison with the Holy Qur’an.

[Kitab-ul-Bariyyah, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 13, pp. 66-67]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 13]

A study of the religions of the world reveals that every religion, except Islam, contains some mistake or the other. This is not because they were all false in their origin, but because after the advent of Islam, God gave up the support of other religions. They became like neglected gardens, which had no gardener to look after them, and for the irrigation and upkeep of which no arrangement had been made, so that gradually they began to decay. Their fruit-bearing trees became dry and barren,

and thorns and weeds spread all over. Those religions lost all spirituality, which is at the root of all religions, and nothing was left but bare words.

God did not allow this to happen in the case of Islam, as
He desired that this garden should flourish throughout.
He made provision in each century for its irrigation and thus rescued it from decay. Although at the beginning of each century, when a man of God was appointed for its reform, the ignorant people opposed him and were averse to the reform of anything which had become part of their habits and customs, yet God Almighty adhered throughout to His way. In these latter days also, which is the time of the last battle between guidance and error, finding the Muslims heedless and neglectful in the beginning of the fourteenth century, God recalled His promise and made provision for the revival of Islam. But other faiths were never revived after the advent of the Holy Prophet
[peace and blessings of Allah be on him] and they all died. There was no spiritual life in them and errors took root in them, as dirt accumulates in a garment which is much in use but which is never washed. People who had no concern with spirituality and who were not free from the stains of earthly existence corrupted these faiths to a degree that they no longer resemble the originals.

Consider the case of Christianity, how pure was its origin. The teaching set forth by Jesus was not perfect as compared with the teachings of the Qur’an, because the time had not yet come for the revelation of the perfect teaching and people were not yet strong enough to bear it, yet that teaching was an excellent one and was appropriate for its own time. It guided to the same God to
Whom the Torah guided; but after Jesus, the god of the

Christians became another god who found no mention in the Torah and was not at all known to the children of
Israel. Belief in this new god upset the whole system of the Torah and all the guidance contained in the Torah for deliverance from sin and attaining true salvation and a pure life was frustrated. Salvation and deliverance from sin now depended upon the confession that Jesus had accepted crucifixion for the sake of the salvation of mankind, and that he was the very God Himself. Many permanent laws of the Torah were abrogated and the
Christian faith was so changed that if Jesus were to come back to the earth he would not be able to recognize it.

It is a matter of surprise that the people who were

admonished to adhere to the Torah set aside its commandments at one stroke. For instance, it is nowhere stated in the Gospel that though the Torah forbids the eating of the flesh of swine yet it is now permitted, nor does the Gospel say that though circumcision is prescribed in the Torah yet that commandment is now abrogated. But all this was done and that which had never been said by Jesus became part of religion. However, as it was God’s design to establish a universal religion, namely Islam, the decay of Christianity was an indication of the appearance of Islam.
It is also well established that Hinduism had been corrupted before the advent of Islam and that throughout
India idol worship had become common. Part of this corruption resulted in the doctrine that God Who is not dependent upon matter for the exercise of His attributes is, according to the Aryas, essentially dependent on the availability of matter for the creation of the universe.
This led to another false doctrine that all particles of matter and all souls are eternal and uncreated. Had they considered deeply the attributes of God, they would never have said so; for if in the exercise of His eternal attribute of creation, God is dependent on matter like a human being, then how is it that in the exercise of the attribute of hearing and seeing He is not so dependent as man is.
Man cannot hear without the agency of air and he cannot see without the aid of light. Then is God also dependent upon light and air for seeing and hearing? If He is not so dependent, be sure that He is not dependent upon matter for the exercise of His attribute of creation. It is entirely false that He is dependent upon matter for the exercise of any of His attributes. It is a great mistake to attribute human weaknesses to God; for instance, that He cannot create something from nothing. Man’s being is limited and God’s Being is unlimited. By the power of His Being, He can create another being. This is the essence of
Godhead. He is not dependent upon matter for the exercise of any of His attributes, for had that been so, He would not be God. Nothing can obstruct Him. If He were to desire to create a heaven and earth instantly, He would be able to do so. Of the Hindus those who, in addition to knowledge, partook of spirituality also and were not committed to bare logic, never believed that concerning
God which the Aryas set forth today. This is the result of the lack of spirituality altogether.

All this corruption, some of which is unmentionable and is opposed to human purity, was an indication of the need of Islam. Every reasonable person is bound to confess that a short while before Islam, all other faiths had become corrupt and had lost all spirituality. The Holy
Prophet [peace and blessings of Allah be on him] was a great reformer in the cause of truth who restored the lost

verities to the world. No Prophet shares with him the pride that he found the whole world in darkness and by his advent that darkness gave place to light.

[Lecture Sialkot, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 20, pp. 203-206]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 14]

wm11657.full:
Introduction

Author: Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian (AS)

Section: Part 1: Islam

When I reflect upon the Holy Word of God, I find that in its teachings it seeks to reform the natural conditions of man and to raise him step by step to higher spiritual levels. In the first place God desires to teach man the elementary rules of behaviour and culture and thus to change him from the wild condition of animals, and then to bestow upon him elementary moral conditions which can be described as culture or civilization. Then He trains him and raises him from the elementary moral conditions to a high moral stage. All this is in truth one stage, which is the reform of natural conditions, and the only difference is one of degree. The All-Wise One has presented the moral system in such a way whereby man should be able to move from a lower moral level to a higher moral level. The third stage is that man should be devoted to winning the true love and pleasure of his Creator and the whole of his being should be devoted to God. It is at this stage that the faith of Muslims has been named Islam, which means to be wholly devoted to God and to keep nothing back.

[Islami Usul ki Philosophy, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 10, p.324]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 12]

Author: Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian (AS)

Section: Part 1: Islam

wm11643.full:
Introduction

In this comprehensive discourse from Essence of Islam (Volume 1), Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (AS), the Promised Messiah and Mahdi, establishes why Islam is the True Religion—contrasting the perfect, exhaustive teachings of the Holy Qur’an with prior scriptures, and demonstrating the living spiritual signs and heavenly support unique to Islam.

Author: Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian (AS)

Section: Part 1: Islam

Remember, to establish its truth, a religion which claims to be from God must prove its excellence in two respects:
First of all, it should be so comprehensive, perfect, complete and free from every defect in its doctrine, teachings and commandments, that reason should not be capable of proposing anything better; and there should be nothing lacking in it. It should be ahead of all other religions in this respect. The Holy Qur’an puts forward this claim by proclaiming:

ٱلۡيَوۡمَ أَكۡمَلۡتُ لَكُمۡ دِينَكُمۡ وَأَتۡمَمۡتُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ نِعۡمَتِي وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ ٱلۡإِسۡلَٰمَ دِينٗا

“This day have I perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you and have chosen for you Islam as religion.” (Surah al-Ma’idah, 5:4)

This means that God requires us to conform to the reality inherent in the word Islam. Here there is a clear claim that the Holy Qur’an comprehends the perfect teaching and that the time of the revelation of the Holy Qur’an was the time when such perfect teaching could be revealed. The Qur’an alone is entitled to make this claim.
No other heavenly book has put forward such a claim.
Both the Torah and the Gospel refrain from making this claim. On the contrary, the Torah sets out God’s commandment that:
“I will raise them up a Prophet from among their brethren, and put My words in his mouth and whosoever will not hearken unto My words I will require it of him.” (Deuteronomy 18:18)

It is obvious, therefore, that if the Torah had been adequate for meeting the needs of subsequent ages, there would have been no necessity for the coming of another
Prophet, listening to whom was made obligatory. In the same way the Gospel has nowhere claimed that its teaching is perfect and comprehensive. But there is a clear confession that:

“I have yet many things to say, but ye cannot bear them now but that when the Paraclete is come he will lead you to the whole truth.” (John 16:12–13)

Thus, Moses confessed the incompleteness of the Torah and drew attention to the teaching of the Prophet who was to come. In the same way, Jesus admitted the incompleteness of his teaching and said that the time had not yet come for the perfect teaching to be disclosed but that when the Paraclete arrives he would set forth the perfect teaching. In contrast the Holy Qur’an does not, like the Torah and the Gospel, leave the matter for another book to complete but announces the perfection of its teaching in the words:

ٱلۡيَوۡمَ أَكۡمَلۡتُ لَكُمۡ دِينَكُمۡ وَأَتۡمَمۡتُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ نِعۡمَتِي وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ ٱلۡإِسۡلَٰمَ دِينٗا

“This day have I perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you and have chosen for you Islam as religion.” (Surah al-Ma’idah, 5:4)

…..Here is thus a great argument in support of Islam that by virtue of its teaching it prevails over every religion and no religion can compete with it in respect of the perfection of its teaching.

The second kind of success, which is peculiar to Islam and not shared by any other religion, and which fully testifies to its truth, is that it manifests its living blessings and miracles of which other religions are wholly deprived. The signs that Islam exhibits not only establish its superiority over other religions but also enable it to draw the hearts of the people by exhibiting its perfect light. The first characteristic of Islam, which we have stated above, that is to say, the perfection of its teaching, is not quite conclusive in establishing that Islam is a true religion revealed by God. A bigoted opponent who is not farsighted may assert that it is possible that a teaching might be perfect and yet it may not proceed from God Almighty. This first characteristic relieves a wise seeker after truth of many doubts and brings him close to certainty, but does not establish the matter conclusively and beyond doubt till it is combined with the second characteristic. When both these characteristics are combined, the light of the true faith reaches its perfection.

A true faith comprises thousands of proofs and lights but these two characteristics are enough to carry conviction to the heart of a seeker after truth and expound the matter to the satisfaction of all deniers of truth. Nothing more is needed in addition. I had originally intended that in support of the truth of Islam I would set down three hundred arguments in Brahin-e-Ahmadiyya. But on further reflection I perceived that these two characteristics are a substitute for thousands of proofs and thus God made me alter my plan.

[Brahin-e-Ahmadiyya, Part V, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 21, pp. 3-6]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 7]

God Almighty is not held back from exposition of the claim of the Holy Prophet [peace and blessings of Allah be on him]. He came like a sun and manifested his light from every point of view. He who turns away from this true sun, will come to no good. We cannot credit such a one with good faith. Can anyone who is afflicted with leprosy and whose limbs are corrupted with leprosy, claim that he is whole and is not in need of treatment?
Should he say so, can we credit him with good faith?
Should such a person insist that he cannot arrive at the truth of Islam, despite good faith and despite every effort such as he puts forth in his worldly affairs, his matter rests with God. We have not come across any such person and we consider it impossible that anyone equipped with reason and a sense of justice should prefer some

other faith to Islam. Foolish and ignorant people adopt the position under the dictates of their lower selves that belief in the Unity of God is enough, and that it is not necessary to follow the Holy Prophet [peace and blessings of Allah be on him]; but it is to be borne in mind that a Prophet is the mother of belief in Unity, who gives birth to it and points to the existence of God. Who knows the exposition of the truth better than God Almighty
Himself? He filled heaven and earth with signs to prove the truth of the Holy Prophet [peace and blessings of
Allah be on him] and now in this age He has sent me and has displayed thousands of signs like heavy rain, which prove the truth of the Holy Prophet [peace and blessings of Allah be on him]. What then is lacking in the full exposition of the truth? He who has sense enough to oppose why can he not think out the way of acceptance? He who pretends that he can see at night, why can he not see in the full light of day? Indeed the way of acceptance is much easier than the way of rejection.

The case of a person whose reason is defective and whose faculties are not normal should be committed to
God, and we have nothing to do concerning him. He is like children who die at an early age. But a wicked denier cannot excuse himself on the ground that he is acting in good faith. It should be considered whether his faculties are such that he can appreciate questions of Unity and
Prophethood. If he is capable of appreciating them and denies out of ill will, he cannot be excused. Can we excuse a person who observes the light of the sun and yet persists in asserting that it is not day but night? In the same way, we cannot excuse those who deliberately indulge in wrong reasoning and are unable to repel the arguments that are put forward on behalf of Islam. Islam

is a living faith. A person who can distinguish between the living and the dead, how can he set aside Islam and accept a dead religion?

[Haqiqat-ul-Wahi, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 22, pp. 180-181]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 10]

Author: Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian (AS)

Section: Part 1: Islam

wm11642.full:
Introduction

Author: Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian (AS)

Section: Part 1: Islam

In order to recognize a true religion it is necessary to look at three matters. In the first place, one must see what is the teaching of a religion concerning God. That is to say, what does a religion state with regard to the Unity, power, knowledge, perfection, greatness, punishment, mercy and other attributes of the Divine…..
Secondly, it is necessary that a seeker after truth should inquire what does a religion teach with regard to his own self and with regard to human conduct. Is there anything in its teaching which would disrupt human relationships, or would draw a person into courses which are inconsistent with modesty and honour, or would be contrary to the law of nature, or would be impossible to conform to or carry out, or make it dangerous to do so. It would also be necessary to see whether some important teaching needed to control disorderliness has been left out. It would also be necessary to discover whether a religion presents God as a Great Benefactor with Whom a relationship of personal love should be established and whether it lays down commandments which lead from darkness into light and from heedlessness to remembrance.
Thirdly, it is necessary for a seeker after truth to satisfy himself that the god presented by a religion should not be one who is believed in on the basis of tales and stories and resembles a dead being. To believe in a god who resembles a dead being, belief in whom is not by virtue of his having manifested himself but is due to one’s own good faith, would be to put him under an obligation. It is

useless to believe in a god whose powers are not felt and who does not himself make manifest the signs of his own existence and life.

[Nasim-e-Da‘wat, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 19, pp. 373-374]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 5]

The religion that claims to be from God must show signs of being from God and should bear God’s seal, which should attest the fact that it is from Him. Islam is such a religion. That God Who is hidden is known through this religion and manifests Himself to the true followers of this religion. A true religion is supported by the hand of
God and through such religion God manifests Himself that He exists. The religions that depend entirely upon stories are only a form of idol worship. Such religions do not possess the spirit of truth. If God is alive as He was, and speaks and hears as He did, there is no reason why
He should continue to be silent as if He does not exist. If
He does not speak in this age, then equally and certainly
He does not hear either. In other words, He is now nothing. That religion alone is true which demonstrates that
God hears and speaks in this age also. In a true religion,
God attests His existence through His speaking.

Search for God is a difficult matter. It is not an affair of worldly philosophers and wise men. Observation of the heavens and earth only leads to the conclusion that although orderliness indicates that the universe should have a Creator yet it is not proof that such a Creator in fact exists. There is a great deal of difference between ought to be and is. The Holy Qur’an is the only book that sets forth His existence as a fact and not only urges the seeking of God but makes Him manifest. There is no other book which makes manifest the Hidden Being.

[Chashma-e-Masihi, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 20, pp. 351-352]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 6]

Religion does not mean disputes, abuse and harsh words that are indulged in, in the name of religion. In this context, no one pays attention to the suppression of inner vices or the establishment of true relationship with the
Beloved. One party attacks another party like dogs and every kind of ill conduct is exhibited in support of religion. Such people do not realize why they came into this world and what is the main purpose of their lives. They continue to be blind and ill-natured and give their bigoted sentiments the name of religion. They exhibit their bad manners and employ their loose tongues in support of a fictitious god of whose existence they have no proof. Of what use is a religion, which does not teach the worship of the Living God? The god that they present is no better than a corpse. He walks with the support of others; when that support is withdrawn, he falls to the ground. The only thing they gain from such a religion is bigotry. They lack altogether true fear of God and true sympathy with mankind, which is the best of characteristics.

[Brahin-e-Ahmadiyya Part V, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 21 p. 28]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 7]

Author: Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian (AS)

Section: Part 1: Islam

wm11641.full:
Introduction

In this foundational discourse from Essence of Islam (Volume 1), Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (AS), the Promised Messiah and Mahdi, expounds upon The Purpose of Religion—demonstrating that true faith is not a matter of lifeless philosophical conjectures or ancient tales, but a living means to attain absolute certainty in God Almighty and salvation from sin.

Author: Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian (AS)

Section: Part 1: Islam

The true purpose of adopting a faith is that one should acquire such certainty concerning God, Who is the fountainhead of salvation, as if one can see Him with one’s eyes. The wicked spirit of sin seeks to destroy a man and a person cannot escape the fatal poison of sin till he believes with full certainty in the Perfect and Living God and till he knows for certain that God exists, Who punishes the offender and bestows upon the righteous everlasting joy. It is a common experience that when one believes in the fatal effects of anything one does not have recourse to it. For instance, no one swallows poison consciously. No one deliberately stands in front of a wild tiger. No one deliberately thrusts his hand into the hole of a serpent. Then why does a person commit sin deliberately? The reason is that he has not that certainty in this matter as he has in other matters of the kind that we have mentioned. The first duty of a person, therefore, is to acquire certainty with regard to the existence of God, and to adopt a religion through which this certainty can be acquired so that he should fear God and shun sin. How can such certainty be acquired? It cannot be acquired through mere stories. It cannot be acquired through mere arguments. The only way of acquiring certainty is to experience God repeatedly through converse with Him or through witnessing His extraordinary signs, or by keeping company with someone who has that experience.

[Nasim-e-Da‘wat, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 19, pp. 447-448]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 3]

The purpose of religion is that man should obtain deliverance from his passions and should develop personal love for God Almighty through certain faith in His existence and His perfect attributes. Such love of God is the paradise, which will appear in diverse shapes in the hereafter. To be unaware of the True God, to keep away from
Him, and not to have any love for Him, is the hell which will appear in diverse shapes in the hereafter. Thus, the true purpose is to have full faith in Him. Now the question is which religion and which book can fulfil this need. The Bible tells us that the door of converse with
God is closed and that the ways of obtaining certainty are sealed. Whatever was to happen, happened in the past and there is nothing in the future….. Of what use then is a religion that is dead? What benefit can we derive from a book that is dead? What grace can be bestowed by a god who is dead?

[Chashma-e-Masihi, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 20, pp. 352-353]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 4]

The purpose of accepting a religion is that God, Who is
Self-Sufficient and is in no need of His creation or its worship, may be pleased with us, and that we should experience such grace and mercy as should wipe out our inner stains and rusts so that our breasts may be filled with certainty and understanding. This is not possible for a man to achieve through his own devices. Therefore,
God the Glorious, keeping hidden mainly His own Being and the wonders of His creation, for instance, souls, bodies, angels, heaven, hell, resurrection, prophethood, etc.

and yet disclosing them partially through reason, appointed his servants to believe in all these mysteries.

[Surmah Chashm Arya, Ruhani Khaza’in, Vol. 2, p. 81]
[Essence of Islam, Vol. 1, p. 4]

Author: Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian (AS)

Introduction

Anti-Ahmadis often quote statements from earlier Hanafi scholars declaring that anyone who claims prophethood after the Holy Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is a disbeliever. The implication is that these statements automatically refute the Ahmadi claim of the Promised Messiah. However, this argument depends upon an important assumption: that these scholars were condemning the exact conception of prophethood that Mirza Ghulam Ahmad claimed. That assumption cannot simply be taken for granted; it has to be demonstrated.

The question is therefore not whether Hanafi scholars condemned the idea of an independent prophet arising after Muhammad ﷺ. Clearly, they did. The real question is whether their statements were intended to condemn the very specific conception of Zillī or Burūzī prophethood claimed by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad: a completely subordinate status, derived from and dependent upon the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, without a new Sharīʿah and without independent prophetic authority.

That distinction is essential.

A Convenient Way of Avoiding the Broader Hanafi Tradition

There is a convenient way in which this argument is sometimes constructed. Rather than engaging with the broader Hanafi intellectual tradition concerning nubuwwah, wilayah, zill, buruz, and the relationship between prophethood and spiritual inheritance, anti-Ahmadi writers go back to isolated Arabic juridical statements from earlier Hanafi authorities and present them as though they settle the entire question.

This conveniently allows them to avoid engaging with the broader Hanafi-Sufi tradition, including later Deobandi and Barelwi scholars as well as major figures who preceded those movements.

More importantly, it allows them to avoid dealing with figures such as Ibn ʿArabi and Mujaddid Alf Thani, whose writings contain discussions highly relevant to the distinction between law-bearing prophethood and subordinate spiritual inheritance.

The point is not that Ibn ʿArabi, Mujaddid Alf Thani, the Deobandis, or the Barelwis were simply “Ahmadi.” They obviously were not. The point is that the Hanafi-Sufi intellectual tradition contains a much more complicated discussion of prophethood, sainthood, spiritual inheritance, and Khatam an-Nabiyyin than the anti-Ahmadi presentation suggests.

For example, Mujaddid Alf Thani is quoted as saying that following the advent of Muhammad ﷺ, the attainment of the attributes of prophethood by his followers “as subordinate or by way of inheritance” does not conflict with his status as the Seal of the Prophets.

Likewise, Ibn ʿArabi distinguishes between the termination of law-bearing prophethood and the broader station of prophethood. He explicitly discusses the end of nubuwwah al-tashrīʿ while explaining that this does not necessarily mean that every dimension associated with the prophetic station has simply ceased to exist.

This is also why the statement of Mawlana Sajid Khan Naqshbandi is relevant. He did not merely acknowledge that Ibn ʿArabi’s passages are difficult or that they require discussion. In addressing one of the difficult passages in Futuhat al-Makkiyyah concerning the continuation of nubuwwah, he explicitly acknowledged the problem by saying, in substance, “we Hanafis have no answer” to it.

That is significant. A prominent Deobandi Hanafi debater is not simply being confronted with an Ahmadi interpretation of Ibn ʿArabi; he himself acknowledges that there is a passage within the writings of a major Hanafi-Sufi authority for which, by his own admission, “we Hanafis have no answer.”

This demonstrates that the matter is not as simple as quoting a few early Hanafi juridical statements and declaring the entire question settled.

The issue is more complicated than that.

The Hanafi Quotations that are brought against us

Let us therefore look at the quotations that are being presented.

Abu Hafs al-Kabir is quoted as saying:

“Likewise, if [someone] were to say, ‘I am the Messenger of Allah,’ or said in Persian, ‘I am a prophet,’ intending by it that he delivers a message, he has disbelieved…”

Jamal ud-Din al-Ghaznawi states:

“Whoever claims prophethood is obligated to repent. If he does not repent, it is obligatory to execute him.”

Ibn Nujaym writes:

“If he isn’t aware that Muhammad ﷺ is the last of the prophets, then he is not a Muslim because [this is known] by necessity.”

Mulla ʿAli al-Qari states:

“The claim of prophethood after our Prophet ﷺ is disbelief by consensus.”

Al-Tahawi likewise writes that Muhammad ﷺ is:

“the Seal of the Prophets…”

and:

“Every claim to prophethood after him is falsehood and deceit.”

These quotations certainly establish that these Hanafi authorities rejected a claim to prophethood after Muhammad ﷺ. There is no need to dispute that point.

The question is what kind of claim were they rejecting?

Were they rejecting the idea that an independent prophet, possessing his own prophetic authority, could arise after Muhammad ﷺ?

Were they rejecting a prophet who brought a new Sharīʿah?

Were they rejecting someone who denied that Muhammad ﷺ was Khatam an-Nabiyyīn?

Or were they also specifically rejecting the concept of a prophet whose entire status is subordinate to, dependent upon, and a manifestation of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ?

The anti-Ahmadi argument must establish this rather than simply assuming it.

But Look at What Mulla ʿAli al-Qari Himself Says

An anti-Ahmadi may try to shut down this distinction by pointing to the strongest-sounding wording in these quotations.

They may say:

“Look, al-Tahawi says, ‘Every claim to prophethood after him is falsehood and deceit,’ and Mulla ʿAli al-Qari says, ‘The claim of prophethood after our Prophet ﷺ is disbelief by consensus.’ What more needs to be explained?”

But there is a serious problem with this argument.

The very same Mulla ʿAli al-Qari who is quoted against Ahmadis also gives a qualification concerning Khatam an-Nabiyyin that is directly relevant to this discussion.

In Al-Asrar al-Marfuʿah fi al-Akhbar al-Mawduʿah, he writes:

ومع هذا لو عاش إبراهيم وصار نبيا، وكذا لو صار عمر نبيا لكانا من أتباعه عليه الصلاة والسلام كعيسى والخضر وإلياس عليهم السلام. فلا يناقض قولَه تعالى: (وخاتم النبيين) إذ المعنى أنه لا يأتي نبي بعده ينسخ ملته ولم يكن من أمته

Had Ibrahim lived and become a prophet, and likewise had Umar become a prophet they would be follower prophets of the Holy Prophet , peace and blesings of Allah be upon him, like Isa, Khidar and Ilyas upon whom all be peace. It does not contradict the divine word ‘Khataman Nabiyyeen’ which means that there shall not be a prophet abrogating his law nor one who was not of his Ummah.[Al-Asrar Al-Marfu’a Fil-Akhbar Al-Mawdu’a, pg. 183]

He gives the hypothetical examples of Ibrahim and ʿUmar becoming prophets and says that, had they become prophets, they would have been followers of Muhammad ﷺ, like ʿIsa, Khidr, and Ilyas. He explicitly says that this would not contradict Khatam an-Nabiyyin because the meaning is that no prophet would come after Muhammad ﷺ who abrogated his religion and was not from his Ummah.

This is extremely significant.

The anti-Ahmadi writer cannot simply quote al-Qari’s statement that “the claim of prophethood after our Prophet ﷺ is disbelief by consensus” and then pretend that al-Qari’s understanding of Khatam an-Nabiyyin contains no qualifications whatsoever.

Al-Qari himself discusses a hypothetical prophet after Muhammad ﷺ who would remain a follower of Muhammad ﷺ and explains Khatam an-Nabiyyin in terms of there being no prophet who would abrogate Muhammad’s law or be outside his Ummah.

Therefore, the discussion is clearly more nuanced than:

“Anyone ever described as a prophet after Muhammad ﷺ = kufr.”

The question is what type of prophethood is being excluded?

And if an anti-Ahmadi responds, “But al-Qari still says that claiming prophethood after Muhammad ﷺ is kufr,” then the answer is simple:

Fine. Explain how that statement is to be reconciled with al-Qari’s own qualification of Khatam an-Nabiyyin.

More importantly, demonstrate that his statement encompasses the specific Ahmadi conception of Zillī/Burūzī prophethood.

That is the actual argument that needs to be made.

The Descent of Jesus ﷺ Creates the Same Problem

There is an even more important issue.

The Jahmiyyah and Muʿtazilah historically objected to the descent of Jesus ﷺ because they believed that his return would conflict with the finality of prophethood. Sunni scholars such as Qadi ʿIyad and Imam al-Nawawi responded to this objection by explaining that Jesus ﷺ does not descend with a law that abrogates the Sharīʿah of Muhammad ﷺ. Rather, he descends as a just judge ruling according to the Sharīʿah of Muhammad ﷺ.

Notice what has happened here.

A Sunni authority is directly confronting the apparent contradiction between:

Khatam an-Nabiyyin

and:

the return of a man who is already a prophet.

The solution is not simply to say:

“Jesus will cease to be a prophet.”

Rather, the solution is to distinguish between independent, law-bearing prophethood and the status of Jesus ﷺ as a prophet who returns while remaining subject to the Sharīʿah of Muhammad ﷺ.

That distinction is fundamental.

Many Sunnis use precisely this distinction to defend the traditional belief in the descent of Jesus ﷺ. They say that Jesus ﷺ does not return as an independent prophet bringing a new Sharīʿah. He returns as a follower of Muhammad ﷺ and rules according to the Sharīʿah of Muhammad ﷺ.

But then an obvious question arises:

When Jesus ﷺ descends, will he still be a prophet?

Will he cease to be a prophet before descending?

Will Allah strip him of his prophethood?

Will the Qur’an and Sunnah suddenly stop describing him as a prophet?

Or will he remain the very same Jesus ﷺ who was already a prophet before the advent of Muhammad ﷺ?

If Jesus ﷺ remains a prophet, then the mere proposition that someone after Muhammad ﷺ can truthfully be called a prophet cannot, by itself, be the complete definition of what constitutes a violation of Khatam an-Nabiyyin.

There must be a distinction concerning what kind of prophethood is meant.

And this is precisely where the anti-Ahmadi argument becomes inconsistent.

When the discussion concerns Jesus ﷺ, the distinction is accepted:

“Yes, Jesus is a prophet, but he is not an independent, law-bearing prophet after Muhammad ﷺ.”

But when the discussion concerns Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, the same distinction is suddenly declared meaningless.

Why?

Mirza Ghulam Ahmad’s Own Explanation

This is where Mirza Ghulam Ahmad’s own writings become decisive, because we should not allow an opponent to define his claim for him.

Mirza Ghulam Ahmad explicitly addressed the accusation that he was claiming the type of prophethood his opponents associated with a post-Muhammadan claimant.

He wrote:

“The aim of this discourse is that while my ignorant opponents accuse me of claiming to be a Prophet or Messenger, I myself make no such claim. I am neither a Prophet nor a Messenger as they think. But I am a Prophet and a Messenger in the way that I have just explained.”

This sentence is crucial.

He does not simply say:

“I am a prophet after Muhammad ﷺ.”

He explicitly says:

“I am neither a Prophet nor a Messenger as they think.”

He then explains the particular sense in which he accepts those terms.

He further states:

“It is only by way of Buruz that I have been made a Prophet and a Messenger…”

And he explains the relationship to Muhammad ﷺ even more explicitly:

“Prophethood and Messengership have not been transferred to anyone else. What belonged to Muhammad ﷺ remains with Muhammad ﷺ.”

This is precisely the distinction that the anti-Ahmadi argument needs to address.

Mirza Ghulam Ahmad was not claiming to be an independent prophet possessing a separate prophetic authority. He was not claiming a new Sharīʿah. He was not claiming to be outside the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ.

His claim was that through Burūz, a person could become a manifestation and reflection of the prophetic reality of Muhammad ﷺ while remaining completely subordinate to him.

Whether one accepts that theological claim is a separate question.

But one cannot refute it merely by proving that Hanafi scholars condemned an independent claim to prophethood unless one first demonstrates that they intended their statements to include this particular subordinate conception.

Mirza Ghulam Ahmad Explicitly Affirms Khatam an-Nabiyyin

Nor can it reasonably be argued that Mirza Ghulam Ahmad simply rejected the finality of prophethood.

In Eik Ghalati Ka Izala, he explicitly rejects the idea of an independent “new” prophet appearing after Muhammad ﷺ. He also rejects the traditional conception of Jesus ﷺ returning as an old prophet who would continue receiving prophetic revelation for forty years after Muhammad ﷺ.

He explicitly affirms the verse:

Khatam an-Nabiyyin

and the hadith:

La nabi ba’di.

He states in substance that no new or old prophet can come after Muhammad ﷺ in the manner imagined by those who believe that Jesus ﷺ will descend as a prophet and continue receiving prophetic revelation for forty years. He calls such a belief false and says that the verse Khatam an-Nabiyyin and the hadith La nabi ba’di testify against it.

This is important because it shows that his argument was not:

“The Qur’an says Muhammad ﷺ is Khatam an-Nabiyyin, but I reject that.”

His argument was precisely the opposite.

He affirmed Khatam an-Nabiyyin and La nabi ba’di while explaining that his own prophetic terminology referred to a subordinate Burūzī manifestation of the Muhammadi prophethood.

That is the actual theological disagreement.

The Difference Between a New Prophet and a Subordinate Prophet

The distinction can therefore be stated very simply.

There are two fundamentally different propositions:

1. A prophet comes after Muhammad ﷺ possessing an independent prophetic office, with authority separate from Muhammad ﷺ and potentially a new or competing Sharīʿah.

2. A person arises from within the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ whose prophetic status is completely subordinate to Muhammad ﷺ, derives from Muhammad ﷺ, does not bring a new Sharīʿah, and is understood as a manifestation or reflection of the Muhammadi prophethood.

The first is precisely the kind of claim that destroys the finality and supremacy of Muhammad ﷺ.

The second is the claim that Ahmadis are actually making.

Therefore, the anti-Ahmadi argument cannot simply collapse both propositions into one category and then quote a ruling against the first as though it automatically disproves the second.

The Broader Sunni Tradition Makes the Issue Even More Difficult

This is why the broader Sunni tradition cannot simply be ignored.

Mulla ʿAli al-Qari himself gives a formulation in which a prophet could hypothetically arise after Muhammad ﷺ while remaining his follower, without contradicting Khatam an-Nabiyyin.

Mujaddid Alf Thani speaks of the attainment of prophetic attributes by followers of Muhammad ﷺ “as subordinate or by way of inheritance” without contradiction to his being Khatam an-Nabiyyin.

Ibn ʿArabi distinguishes the termination of law-bearing prophethood from the broader prophetic station.

ʿAbd al-Wahhab al-Shaʿrani likewise gives the formulation that the statements of the Holy Prophet ﷺ concerning there being no prophet or messenger after him mean that there will be no law-bearing prophet after him.

Shah Waliullah al-Dehlawi likewise explains La nabi ba’di in connection with the absence of a prophet who would bring a new law or Sharīʿah.

And Sunni scholars defending the descent of Jesus ﷺ have had to explain that his return does not violate Khatam an-Nabiyyin because he does not return with an abrogating law.

Again, this does not prove Ahmadiyyat by itself.

What it does prove is that the simplistic equation:

“Any use of the word prophet after Muhammad ﷺ = the exact kufr condemned by every Hanafi authority”

is not historically or conceptually sufficient.

The terminology requires explanation.

What About the Strongest Hanafi Statements?

At this point, an opponent may return to the strongest wording:

“But Abu Hafs said it is kufr.”

“Ghaznawi said the claimant must repent.”

“Ibn Nujaym said that denying Muhammad ﷺ as the last prophet makes a person a disbeliever.”

“Al-Qari said it is kufr by consensus.”

“Al-Tahawi said every claim after him is falsehood.”

None of these quotations should simply be ignored.

But neither should they be treated as if they magically answer the disputed question.

For example, Ibn Nujaym’s statement is especially important because it explicitly connects disbelief with failure to recognize Muhammad ﷺ as the last of the prophets. That raises the question: what does “last of the prophets” mean in the broader Hanafi-Sunni interpretive tradition?

If Mulla ʿAli al-Qari can explain Khatam an-Nabiyyin in a manner that excludes a prophet who abrogates Muhammad’s law and is outside his Ummah, then the meaning of “last” and the meaning of “prophet after him” require further examination.

Likewise, if Mujaddid Alf Thani can speak about followers of Muhammad ﷺ attaining the attributes of prophethood “as subordinate or by way of inheritance” without contradicting his being Khatam an-Nabiyyin, then the category of subordinate prophetic manifestation cannot simply be ignored.

And if Ibn ʿArabi can distinguish the termination of law-bearing prophethood from the prophetic station, while a prominent Deobandi Hanafi debater himself admits that “we Hanafis have no answer” to a difficult passage on this issue, then it is clear that the intellectual history is not as straightforward as the anti-Ahmadi argument suggests.

The Wahhabi/Salafi Point: Hanafiyyat aur Mirzaiyyat

There is another interesting point that the anti-Ahmadi argument conveniently overlooks. Even Wahhabi and Salafi anti-Ahmadi literature has recognized that the relationship between Hanafi teachings and Ahmadiyyat is not as straightforward as simply saying, “Hanafis reject Ahmadis.”

A work titled Hanafiyyat aur Mirzaiyyat was written from an anti-Ahmadi Wahhabi/Salafi perspective precisely to examine the similarities and parallels between Hanafi teachings and Ahmadi beliefs. The very existence of such a work is significant. Why would an anti-Ahmadi Wahhabi author need to devote an entire work to comparing Hanafi teachings with Mirzaiyyat if the two were simply and fundamentally opposed on the question of the finality of prophethood?

This becomes especially relevant when Mulla ʿAli al-Qari is repeatedly quoted as though one isolated statement from him settles the entire question. If the Hanafi tradition is being invoked as the decisive authority against Ahmadiyyat, then its broader teachings and internal distinctions also have to be considered.

In other words, the argument cannot simply be:

“Here are five Hanafi quotations against claiming prophethood after Muhammad ﷺ. Therefore, the Ahmadi position is automatically refuted.”

The proper question is:

“Do these quotations actually address and condemn the specific Zillī/Burūzī conception of prophethood claimed by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad?”

If the answer is supposed to be yes, that needs to be demonstrated—not merely assumed.

Indeed, the fact that anti-Ahmadi Wahhabi/Salafi literature itself has devoted attention to comparing Hanafiyyat and Mirzaiyyat should make us cautious about presenting the Hanafi tradition as though it were a monolithic body of thought whose every formulation can be reduced to a single anti-Ahmadi slogan.

Maulana Muhammad Ahsan Amrohi’s Detailed Answer to the Objection

This objection was directly addressed by Maulana Sayyid Muhammad Ahsan of Amroha, one of the foremost scholars of the Ahmadiyya Movement and a scholar who, on the instructions of Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, would respond to the allegations of opponents.

A few days after the publication of Aik Ghalati Ka Izala, Maulana Muhammad Ahsan informed Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad that he had received a letter from Hafiz Muhammad Yusuf, who had heard that Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad had claimed to be a prophet in the pamphlet—meaning, in the conception of non-Ahmadi Muslims, a Mustaqil (independent/autonomous) or Shari‘i (law-bearing) Nabi appearing after the Holy Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad instructed Maulana Ahsan to answer the allegation in detail so that his beliefs would be clearly conveyed.

The resulting letter, dated 21 November 1901, was published in Al-Hakam on 24 November 1901 and extended over six pages. The editor described it as a detailed exposition of Aik Ghalati Ka Izala. Maulana Ahsan’s response is particularly relevant because he did not merely offer a general defense. He went through Aik Ghalati Ka Izala and listed nineteen separate passages in which Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad explicitly denied the very conception of prophethood that Hafiz Muhammad Yusuf was attributing to him.

Maulana Ahsan begins by stating that the pamphlet itself contains clear and explicit denials of the alleged claim:

“There certainly cannot come any prophet, new or old, in the way in which…”

He then points out that it states:

“Such a belief is undoubtedly a sin, and the verse ‘He is the Messenger of Allah and the Khatam an-nabiyyin’ along with the hadith ‘there is no prophet after me’ are conclusive proof of the absolute falsity of this view.”

Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad further says:

“I, however, am strongly opposed to such beliefs.”

and:

“I … have true and full faith in the statement.”

referring to the doctrine of Khatam an-Nabiyyin.

The pamphlet then explains the distinction upon which the Ahmadi position rests:

“After the Holy Prophet Muhammad, the doors of prophecies have been closed till the Day of Judgment. … But one window, that of the path of Siddiq, is open, namely, fana fir-rasul.”

Maulana Ahsan explains this fana fir-rasul as perfect successorship to the Holy Prophet ﷺ, which is also described as Burūz or manifestation.

The pamphlet further states:

“It is not possible now for a Hindu or a Jew or a Christian or a nominal Muslim to apply the word nabi to himself.”

and:

“All the windows of prophethood have been closed.”

The distinction becomes even more explicit when Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad states:

“After our Holy Prophet Muhammad till the Day of Judgment, there is no prophet to whom a new Shariah is to be revealed.”

and:

“And whoever makes such a claim indeed commits heresy.”

He then applies this distinction directly to himself:

“I have not brought a Shariah independently.”

“Nor am I a prophet in my own right.”

“I am not a possessor of Shariah.”

He further explains:

“All these graces have not been bestowed upon me without mediation, but that there is a holy being in heaven, namely, Muhammad Mustafa, whose spiritual benefit I have received.”

Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad then returns to the doctrine of Khatam an-Nabiyyin:

“In other words, the term Khatam an-Nabiyyin is a Divine seal which has been put upon the prophethood of the Holy Prophet. It is not possible now that this seal could ever break.”

And:

“A seal has been put upon prophethood till the Day of Judgment.”

Finally, he directly addresses the allegation:

“Ignorant opponents accuse me of claiming to be a prophet and messenger. I make no such claim.”

He clarifies:

“I am neither a prophet nor a messenger in the sense which they have in mind.”

and concludes:

“Hence the person who maliciously accuses me of claiming prophethood and messengership is a liar and evil-minded.”

Maulana Ahsan therefore asks, in substance, how a person whose writing repeatedly denies autonomous prophethood (Nabuwaat-Mustaqil) can reasonably be accused of claiming autonomous prophethood ( (Nabuwaat-Mustaqil). He asks the critic whether, “if you have any fear of God in you,” he can really describe someone whose writing repeatedly denies such a claim as a claimant to that very thing.

He then asks:

“Or, can any sane adult say that this fana fir-rasul has claimed that prophethood and messengership which is denied by the consensus of opinion of the entire Muslim Umma?”

This is the central issue. Maulana Ahsan is not denying the finality of prophethood. He is arguing that the finality of prophethood must not be confused with the spiritual graces that flow from the Khatam an-Nabiyyin.

The Distinction Between Khatam an-Nabiyyin and Its Spiritual Graces

Maulana Ahsan then introduces what he calls certain principles accepted by the major authorities of the Muslim Ummah. Among these is the principle that members of the Muslim Ummah can receive Divine communications and knowledge of the unseen.

He then explains his understanding of the terminology of nabi and rasul, and connects this with the fact that Hafiz Muhammad Yusuf had already accepted Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad as a Mujaddid and had accepted his revelations.

From this he argues that the issue is not whether Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad was claiming the independent prophethood of a new law-bearing prophet. Rather, the issue is whether a person who is completely subordinate to Muhammad ﷺ can be described as a nabi or rasul by way of reflection (zill).

Maulana Ahsan writes:

“The first point is the confirmation and establishment of the doctrine of Khatam an-nabiyyin, which has the highest precedence. The second point, which is a branch of the first one, is the proof and establishment of the benefits and blessings of the Khatam an-nabiyyin, which in other words is known as prophethood by way of reflection, partial messengership or the burooz of Muhammad.”

He then emphasizes that these two ideas are connected:

“Though these two concepts are mutually dependent, but unless the first one is established and proved, the second one cannot be proved.”

This is important for understanding his argument. The Burūz of Muhammad ﷺ is not presented as a rival to Khatam an-Nabiyyin. It is presented as a consequence and manifestation of it.

Bayazid Bustami and the Language of Burūz

Maulana Ahsan then turns to examples from the spiritual tradition of Islam. This is one of the most striking portions of his letter because he does not merely assert that the concept of Burūz exists—he gives examples of earlier Muslim saints using remarkably strong prophetic language.

He writes:

“There is a hadith: ‘The ulama of my Umma are like the prophets of the Israelites.’”

He then cites another report:

“Whomever death overtakes while he is searching for knowledge with which to revive Islam, there is only one degree between him and the prophets in heaven.”

Maulana Ahsan then asks:

“Now I ask you: do you think that the Mahdi and the Promised Messiah is no greater at all than that seeker of knowledge who seeks knowledge in order to revive Islam?”

He then gives an even more striking example:

“Hazrat Ali has also been called the burooz of the Messiah by the Holy Prophet.”

But the most interesting example is his reference to Bayazid Bustami:

“It is written in Tazkirat-ul-Auliya that Hazrat Bayazid Bustami said: I am Adam, I am Seth, I am Noah, I am Abraham, I am Moses, I am Jesus, I am Muhammad.”

Maulana Ahsan immediately explains why he considers this relevant:

“It is worth remembering here that Bayazid Bustami has made this claim to be burooz by himself. There is no specific prophecy about him made by the Holy Prophet.”

His argument is therefore that Muslim mystical literature already contained examples of saints describing themselves in the language of manifestation or identification with earlier prophets. The significance, according to Ahsan, is not that Bayazid Bustami literally became an independent Adam, Noah, Moses, Jesus, or Muhammad. Rather, he was speaking in the language of Burūz and spiritual identification.

Ahsan then contrasts this with the Promised Messiah:

“But the Holy Prophet has himself given the Promised Mahdi the names Muhammad and Ahmad in his sayings.”

He continues:

“Even more interesting is that in Barahin Ahmadiyya both these names are to be found in revelations. Thus the hadith confirms the revelation, and the revelation confirms the hadith.”

And he adds:

“The name Ahmad was given to him even at birth as a mark of respect and honour for the Holy Prophet Muhammad, that is: Ghulam Ahmad.”

Maulana Ahsan’s point is that the name Muhammad or Ahmad applied to the Promised Messiah is not being understood merely as an ordinary personal name. He argues that it points to the spiritual reality of Burūz:

“It is obvious that by the giving of the name [in hadith] is not meant the name merely as a word, for hundreds of children are given the names Ahmad and Muhammad. Here by names Muhammad and Ahmad is meant the true nature underlying these names.”

Ibn Arabi and the Concept of Spiritual Union

Maulana Ahsan then gives another example from Ibn Arabi. He writes:

“Muhyuddin Ibn Arabi writes in Futuhat that he saw the Holy Prophet Muhammad in a dream, in which Imam Abu Muhammad Ibn Hazm embraced the Holy Prophet and disappeared into him, so that there was none there except the Holy Prophet Muhammad.”

He identifies this as an example of what he calls ittihad or union, explaining that the person appearing as Burūz can be a Mujaddid who is completely self-effaced in the Holy Prophet ﷺ.

This is important because it demonstrates the conceptual framework Ahsan Amrohi is using. His argument is not simply that the word nabi can be redefined whenever convenient. Rather, he is appealing to a broader Islamic mystical vocabulary in which saints and spiritual figures could be described through their complete identification with, manifestation of, or self-effacement in earlier prophets.

He therefore argues that the Promised Messiah’s claim should be understood within this framework rather than through the definition of a Mustaqil or Shari‘i prophet who establishes an independent religious law.

Why Did the Early Muslims Not Use This Terminology?

Maulana Ahsan then addresses the obvious question: if this type of zillī or Burūzī prophethood was possible, why did the Companions and early generations not openly call themselves nabi or rasul?

His answer is that there were two distinct stages.

The first was the establishment of the doctrine of Khatam an-Nabiyyin. Because false claimants such as Musaylimah had appeared, the early Muslims’ attention was directed toward firmly establishing the finality of Muhammad ﷺ and eliminating the false claims of independent prophets.

Once this doctrine had become firmly established throughout the Muslim Ummah, Maulana Ahsan argues, the time came for the blessings and spiritual graces of that finality to be manifested.

He writes:

“When belief in the finality of prophethood had become well fixed in the minds of the entire Umma, then came the time for the proof and demonstration of those graces and blessings of the finality of prophethood.”

He therefore sees the appearance of the Promised Messiah not as a challenge to Khatam an-Nabiyyin, but as a demonstration of its spiritual consequences.

He connects this to the names Muhammad and Ahmad given to the Promised Mahdi, arguing that these names point toward the Burūz of Muhammad ﷺ.

The Continuing Blessings of Khatam an-Nabiyyin

Maulana Ahsan then asks a broader theological question:

“If the blessings of the finality of prophethood cannot be attained, by way of reflection, by its worthy, perfect and sincere followers, then how can the reform of the Umma and the revival of the religion of Islam take place?”

He continues:

“Which accomplishment of the Khatam an-nabiyyin, the head of the messengers, will remain in the world, if all those doors of graces and Divine blessings which were open for the Israelites are closed and all blessings from the Holy Prophet Muhammad have come to an end?”

He then interprets Qur’an 33:40 in this context, arguing that the Holy Prophet’s status as Khatam an-Nabiyyin does not mean that his spiritual influence and blessings cease after his physical life. Rather, those blessings continue to reach the perfect members of his Ummah.

He writes:

“The graces of his messengership and the blessings of his finality of prophethood will continue till the Day of Judgment.”

And he identifies these blessings with:

“Juzwi prophethood and messengership by way of reflection.”

*Note: Ahsan Amrohi RA referred to Juzwi nabis as actual prophets See: Lahori Ahmadi Elders Affirming Prophethood of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad AS

He then connects this specifically to the Promised Messiah:

“And in the last days a Mahdi will arise who will be ‘Muhammad’ and ‘Ahmad’.”

The Significance of These Examples

Maulana Ahsan’s examples are important because they show exactly how he understood the terminology being used.

He cites the ulama being compared to the prophets of Israel.

He cites a seeker of knowledge being only one degree removed from the prophets in heaven.

He cites Hadhrat Ali being described as the Burūz of the Messiah.

He cites Bayazid Bustami saying:

“I am Adam, I am Seth, I am Noah, I am Abraham, I am Moses, I am Jesus, I am Muhammad.”

And he cites Ibn Arabi describing Ibn Hazm as disappearing into the Holy Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

None of these examples are presented as claims to independent, law-bearing prophethood. Rather, they illustrate the language of spiritual manifestation, identification, and fana fi’r-Rasul that Maulana Ahsan believes provides the proper framework for understanding the Promised Messiah.

That is why his response to the Hanafi objection is significant.

The Hanafi quotations may condemn someone who says, in the ordinary sense, “I am an independent prophet after Muhammad ﷺ.” But that is precisely the conception Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad repeatedly rejected.

The Ahmadi claim, as explained by Maulana Ahsan, is instead that the Promised Messiah is a Burūz of Muhammad ﷺ, a perfect reflection of the Khatam an-Nabiyyin whose spiritual status exists only through complete subordination to him.

Therefore, the anti-Ahmadi argument still has to establish the crucial point: that the Hanafi authorities intended their condemnations to include this specific Burūzī and Zillī conception, rather than the independent or Shari‘i prophethood that Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad explicitly rejected.

Simply quoting a Hanafi scholar saying that “whoever claims prophethood after Muhammad ﷺ is a disbeliever” does not, by itself, answer that question. The entire dispute is over what kind of prophethood is being claimed and what kind of prophethood those Hanafi statements were condemning.

Importantly, this detailed explanation by Maulana Sayyid Muhammad Ahsan of Amroha was not merely his own private interpretation. Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad himself instructed him to write a “very detailed and clear letter” so that his beliefs could be properly conveyed to the opponent. The resulting six-page letter was then published in Al-Hakam as a detailed exposition of Aik Ghalati Ka Izala. The editorial introduction described it as an “invaluable letter” and a “fine exposition” of the pamphlet, stating that it contained “truth and knowledge” and that the scholar was speaking “with the support of the Holy Spirit.” Thus, the explanation given by Maulana Ahsan was published with the approval and direction of Hadhrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad and presented as an authoritative explanation of the position expressed in Aik Ghalati Ka Izala.

The Anti-Ahmadi Argument Still Has to Prove the Crucial Point

The burden of proof therefore lies with the anti-Ahmadi argument.

If you quote Mulla ʿAli al-Qari, explain his complete position.

If you quote al-Tahawi, explain precisely what category of prophetic claim he was condemning.

If you quote Ibn Nujaym, explain whether his statement is directed against someone denying that Muhammad ﷺ is Khatam an-Nabiyyin in the sense understood by the Sunni creed, or whether it explicitly addresses the technical distinction Ahmadis make.

If you quote Abu Hafs al-Kabir, explain the context and the type of prophetic claim being discussed.

And if you invoke “ijmaʿ,” demonstrate that the alleged consensus actually encompasses the specific technical conception of Zillī/Burūzī prophethood rather than simply assuming that it does.

Otherwise, the argument becomes circular.

The reasoning becomes:

The Hanafi scholars said a claimant to prophethood after Muhammad ﷺ is a disbeliever.”

Then:

“Mirza Ghulam Ahmad claimed prophethood.”

Therefore:

“Mirza Ghulam Ahmad is a disbeliever.”

But the entire disputed issue lies between those two premises:

What did “claiming prophethood after Muhammad ﷺ” mean in the Hanafi statements, and does that definition encompass Mirza Ghulam Ahmad’s particular claim?

That is precisely what must be proved.

Conclusion

The real question is not whether Muhammad ﷺ is Khatam an-Nabiyyin.

Ahmadis affirm this.

It is not whether an independent prophet carrying a new Sharīʿah can come after him.

Ahmadis reject this.

It is not whether someone can appear after Muhammad ﷺ possessing an independent prophetic office that competes with or supersedes him.

Ahmadis reject this as well.

And it is not even whether Jesus ﷺ can return with a new Sharīʿah after Muhammad ﷺ.

Ahmadis reject that conception too.

The actual point of disagreement is whether a completely subordinate, non-law-bearing, Zillī/Burūzī manifestation of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ can be described as nubuwwah without violating Khatam an-Nabiyyin.

And ironically, the Sunni explanation of the return of Jesus ﷺ already requires a distinction between prophethood itself and independent, law-bearing prophethood after Muhammad ﷺ.

If Jesus ﷺ can remain a prophet while appearing after Muhammad ﷺ because he does not bring a new law and remains subordinate to the Sharīʿah of Muhammad ﷺ, then the anti-Ahmadi cannot simply end the discussion by saying:

“There is no prophet after Muhammad ﷺ.”

They have to explain what “prophet” means in the particular case being discussed.

That is precisely the distinction Ahmadis are asking them to address.

The Hanafi quotations therefore do not settle the debate merely by being quoted. They establish that a particular conception of post-Muhammadan prophethood was condemned. The real question is whether that condemned category is identical to the conception Mirza Ghulam Ahmad actually claimed.

And that is the question the anti-Ahmadi argument still has to answer.
